cp-mullane.summary: Before a proceeding is accorded finality, due process requires notice reasonably calculated, under all the circumstances, to apprise interested parties and give them a chance to object; publication sufficed for beneficiaries who could not be identified or located with due diligence, but known present beneficiaries with addresses on the trustee’s books were entitled at least to ordinary mail.

sections.Parties: Central Hanover Bank and Trust Company, a New York trust company, was trustee of a common trust fund and petitioned the Surrogate’s Court to settle its first account; in the Supreme Court it was an appellee. Mullane, the appellant, had been appointed special guardian and attorney for all persons, known or unknown, with a present or future interest in the fund’s income; Vaughan, also an appellee, represented those interested in principal. The beneficiaries themselves never appeared. The trustee sought a decree binding every beneficiary; Mullane objected that they had not received constitutionally adequate notice.
sections.Material Facts: New York Banking Law § 100-c let a trust company pool the assets of many small trusts into one investment fund; a decree settling the periodic account bound everyone with an interest in the fund and cut off claims against the trustee for mismanagement during the period. Central Hanover established its fund in January 1946 and petitioned in March 1947 to settle its first account; 113 trusts participated, about half inter vivos and half testamentary, with capital near three million dollars, and some beneficiaries lived outside New York. The only notice was the statutory one: publication in a local newspaper for four successive weeks giving the company’s name, the fund’s name and date and a list of participating trusts, naming no beneficiary. When each trust entered the fund the company had mailed known adult income beneficiaries a copy of the statute, months or years earlier.
sections.Procedural History: Mullane appeared specially and objected that the statutory notice was inadequate under the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, so the Surrogate’s Court lacked jurisdiction to enter a binding decree. The Surrogate overruled the objections and entered a final decree accepting the account; the Appellate Division and the New York Court of Appeals affirmed, holding the notice constitutionally sufficient. The case came to the Supreme Court on appeal, the route then available when a state’s highest court upheld a state statute against a federal constitutional challenge. Justice Jackson wrote for the Court; Justice Burton dissented; Justice Douglas took no part. The Court reversed and remanded on April 24, 1950.
sections.Issue: Could New York bind beneficiaries who lived outside the state and were never personally served, when the decree adjudicated their personal claims against the trustee rather than title to specific property? If so, was newspaper publication constitutionally adequate for each class of beneficiary: those whose interests or whereabouts could not be found with due diligence, those whose interests were conjectural or future, and known present beneficiaries whose addresses the trustee had on its books?
sections.Holding: New York’s power did not depend on labeling the proceeding in rem, quasi in rem or in personam; its interest in closing trusts that exist by the grace of its laws and are administered under its courts’ supervision let it determine the interests of all claimants, resident or not, provided the procedure gave them a full opportunity to be heard. Due process requires notice reasonably calculated, under all the circumstances, to apprise interested parties of the pendency of the action and afford them an opportunity to object. Publication sufficed for beneficiaries whose interests or whereabouts could not be ascertained with due diligence and for conjectural or future interests; it failed for known present beneficiaries of known residence, who were entitled at least to ordinary mail. Personal service was not required.
sections.Reasoning: The Court declined to decide by classification: accounting proceedings had been called in rem, quasi in rem and in the nature of in rem, and the Fourteenth Amendment does not depend on a classification so elusive. Power gave way to opportunity: an adjudication that deprives a person of property must be preceded by notice and a hearing appropriate to the case, and when notice is a person’s due, process which is a mere gesture is not due process. The means chosen must be such as one desirous of actually informing the absentee might reasonably adopt: reasonably certain to inform, or, where that is impossible, not substantially less likely to succeed than feasible substitutes. Publication is a feint for known persons, since chance alone brings a back-page notice to a reader and this one named no beneficiary. For known beneficiaries with addresses on the trustee’s books, the mails were cheap and efficient, the class shared identical interests so notice to most protected all, and fiction should not deny the fair play secured only by close adhesion to fact.

cp-mullane.separateOpinions: Justice Burton dissented: common trusts exist only where the instruments creating the participating trusts permit them, and whether notice beyond the statutory publication and court-appointed representation should be required was a matter for the state’s discretion. Justice Douglas took no part.

cp-szukhent.summary: A stranger named in a printed lease to receive process for the lessees was an “agent authorized by appointment” under the Federal Rules once she promptly accepted the papers and mailed them to the lessees; the Court expressly left open the case in which the appointed agent gives no prompt notice.

sections.Parties: National Equipment Rental, Ltd., a corporation with its principal place of business in New York, leased farm equipment to the respondents and was the plaintiff below and petitioner. The Szukhents, a father and son farming in Michigan, were the lessees, defendants and respondents. Florence Weinberg, the person the lease designated to receive process for them in New York, was not a party. The lessor wanted to sue in New York for unpaid rent; the Szukhents sought to quash service on the ground that Weinberg was not their agent.
sections.Material Facts: In 1961 the Szukhents leased farm equipment on a printed form less than a page and a half long, with eighteen numbered paragraphs. The last paragraph, printed just above their signatures in the same type as the rest, deemed the agreement made in Nassau County, New York, chose New York law, and designated Florence Weinberg, of 47-21 Forty-first Street, Long Island City, as agent for the purpose of accepting service of any process within New York. The Szukhents did not know her; the company had chosen her, and it emerged after suit that she was the wife of one of its officers. In 1962 the company sued in federal court in New York alleging missed rental payments. A marshal delivered two copies of the summons and complaint to Weinberg, who mailed them to the Szukhents the same day with a letter saying she had been served as their agent.
sections.Procedural History: The District Court for the Eastern District of New York quashed service: although Weinberg had promptly notified the Szukhents and sent the papers, the lease did not explicitly require her to do so, so there was a failure of the agency arrangement to achieve intrinsic and continuing reality. The Second Circuit affirmed, 311 F.2d 79. The Supreme Court granted certiorari and reversed and remanded on January 6, 1964. Justice Stewart wrote for a five-Justice majority; Justice Black dissented alone, and Justice Brennan, joined by Chief Justice Warren and Justice Goldberg, dissented separately. The question arose under Rule 4(d)(1), now Rule 4(e)(2)(C).
sections.Issue: Was a person designated in a printed lease to receive process for the lessees, who was a stranger to them and whose appointment did not expressly require her to forward process, an agent authorized by appointment to receive service under the Federal Rules, where she in fact promptly transmitted the summons and complaint to them?
sections.Holding: Yes. Parties to a contract may agree in advance to submit to a court’s jurisdiction, to permit notice to be served by the opposing party, or even to waive notice altogether. Under general agency principles, Weinberg’s prompt acceptance and transmittal of the papers validated the agency without an express promise to forward them, so service on her was valid. The Rule sets a uniform federal standard, and neither Michigan nor New York law required an express undertaking to notify the principal. The holding was confined to the case in which prompt notice was actually given; the Court did not reach a case in which the defendant received no personal notice.
sections.Reasoning: The Court first set aside Wuchter v. Pizzutti, which concerned the Fourteenth Amendment limits on a state statute designating a public official to receive process for nonresidents; the question here was whether a private contract could appoint an agent within the meaning of a Federal Rule. The clause’s purpose was plain: the company inserted it, and the Szukhents agreed, so that litigation under the lease would take place in New York, and it was settled that contracting parties may agree in advance to jurisdiction, to service by the adversary, or to waive notice altogether. Applying general agency law, Weinberg’s prompt acceptance and transmittal of the papers under the authority the lease conferred was itself sufficient to validate the agency even without an advance promise to forward process. The alleged conflict of interest ignored the narrow agency: Weinberg was appointed for the single purpose of receiving service, both sides shared an interest in timely notice, and nothing suggested she had a pecuniary stake. Had she not promptly notified the Szukhents, a claim might well be made that her failure invalidated the agency.

cp-szukhent.separateOpinions: Justice Black dissented: the Szukhents had never heard of Weinberg, the company handpicked her, and only after suit did it emerge that she was an officer’s wife; the appointment was invalid under New York law, and calling their signature knowing consent to suit in New York was “a fiction—not even an amiable one.” He predicted such clauses would spread through the boilerplate of equipment leases and conditional sales contracts. Justice Brennan, joined by Chief Justice Warren and Justice Goldberg, would have required no conflicting interest, an explicit condition that the agent transmit process forthwith, and proof beyond a signature that an individual understandingly consented to be sued away from home.

cp-wyman.summary: Fraud that lures a defendant into the forum so that he can be served defeats jurisdiction over his person, so the resulting judgment is void, is not entitled to full faith and credit, and may be attacked collaterally when the plaintiff sues on it elsewhere without the defendant having appeared or defended in the rendering state.

sections.Parties: Wyman, the appellant, had obtained a default judgment against Newhouse in a Florida state court and sued in federal court in New York to enforce it. Newhouse, the appellee, was a New York resident who had never lived in Florida; he contended that the Florida court never acquired jurisdiction over him because he had been tricked into entering Florida to be served. Judge Manton wrote for a Second Circuit panel that included Judges Learned Hand and Swan.
sections.Material Facts: Wyman and Newhouse, both married, had carried on an affair for some years; Wyman’s husband had since died. On October 25, 1935, while Newhouse was in Salt Lake City, he received her telegram: “Account illness home planning leaving. Please come on way back. Must see you.” A letter followed saying her mother was dying in Ireland and that she was leaving the United States for good but could not go without seeing him once more; she repeated this by telephone in a distressed voice, arranged accommodations in Miami by telegram. When he landed at the Miami airport at six in the morning, Wyman stood with her sister about 75 feet away, a deputy sheriff served him with process in a suit for $500,000 for money loaned, money advanced and seduction under promise of marriage. He flew home that evening and, on counsel’s advice, ignored the summons; a default judgment followed.
sections.Procedural History: Wyman sued on the Florida judgment in federal court in New York. Newhouse moved to dismiss before trial under Rule 113 of the New York Rules of Civil Practice, the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure not yet being in effect, and the motion was decided on affidavits. The district court dismissed the complaint. The Second Circuit affirmed on December 6, 1937, 93 F.2d 313, and the Supreme Court denied certiorari, 303 U.S. 664 (1938).
sections.Issue: Must a New York court give effect to a Florida default judgment when the Florida court obtained personal jurisdiction by serving a defendant whom the plaintiff fraudulently induced to enter Florida? May the defendant raise the fraud as a defense to enforcement in New York without having challenged service or defended on the merits in Florida?
sections.Holding: No, and yes. Fraud that induces a defendant to come within a court’s territorial jurisdiction so that he may be served defeats the court’s jurisdiction over his person; a fraud affecting jurisdiction is equivalent to a lack of jurisdiction, so the judgment is void and not binding when the plaintiff seeks to enforce it in another state. The defendant need not attack the judgment in the rendering state or defend on the merits there; he may raise the fraud as an equitable defense when sued on the judgment, and the enforcing court may consider the jurisdictional question collaterally. The dismissal was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: The affidavits and the reasonable inferences from them convincingly showed that Newhouse was induced to enter Florida by fraud: Wyman falsely represented her mother’s illness, her departure from the country and her affection when her sole purpose was to bring him within reach of Florida process. Service on a person physically present in a state ordinarily confers personal jurisdiction under Pennoyer v. Neff, but the court treated fraud as an exception: Newhouse’s presence was the product of deception, and a fraud affecting jurisdiction is the equivalent of a lack of jurisdiction, so the judgment procured by it was null and void. The Full Faith and Credit Clause and its implementing statute, now 28 U.S.C. § 1738, require each state to give sister-state judgments the effect they have where rendered, but a judgment rendered without jurisdiction over the defendant is not entitled to that effect. Newhouse had no obligation to go back to Florida to attack the judgment or to defend on the merits there; a judgment entered without jurisdiction may be attacked collaterally in the later enforcement proceeding, so his equitable defense sufficed.

cp-sniadach.summary: Prejudgment garnishment of wages on a clerk-issued summons, with no notice or hearing before the wages are frozen, violates due process absent extraordinary circumstances, because wages are a specialized form of property whose interim loss can drive a wage-earning family to the wall.

sections.Parties: Christine Sniadach, a wage earner, was the defendant in the garnishment action and the petitioner. Family Finance Corporation of Bay View, the creditor, was the plaintiff and a respondent. Her employer, Miller Harris Instrument Co., was named as garnishee, the third party holding money owed to the debtor. The creditor sought to freeze part of her wages pending trial of its claim; Sniadach sought dismissal of the garnishment as a denial of due process.
sections.Material Facts: Family Finance began a garnishment action on a claim of $420 on a promissory note. The employer answered that it held $63.18 in wages earned by Sniadach and not yet paid; it would pay half to her as a subsistence allowance and hold the other half, $31.59, subject to the court’s order. Under Wisconsin’s procedure the clerk of court issued the garnishment summons at the request of the creditor’s lawyer; service on the garnishee froze the wages, and the creditor then had ten days to serve the summons and complaint on the debtor. The wages stayed frozen until the main suit was tried, and the debtor could free them only by winning on the merits. She had no opportunity to be heard before the freeze.
sections.Procedural History: Sniadach moved to dismiss the garnishment on the ground that the procedure violated the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment because it provided no notice or hearing before the wages were taken. The Wisconsin courts rejected the challenge, and the Wisconsin Supreme Court sustained the procedure, 37 Wis. 2d 163 (1967). The Supreme Court granted certiorari and reversed on June 9, 1969. Justice Douglas wrote for the Court; Justice Harlan concurred; Justice Black dissented.
sections.Issue: Does a state procedure that permits a creditor to freeze a debtor’s wages through garnishment before trial, without notice to the debtor or an opportunity to be heard, violate the Due Process Clause?
sections.Holding: Yes. Wages are a specialized type of property presenting distinct problems in the economic system, and prejudgment garnishment of the Wisconsin type is a taking that may impose tremendous hardship on wage earners with families to support. Summary procedures may satisfy due process in extraordinary situations, but Wisconsin’s statute was not narrowly drawn to meet any such situation and none was present. Absent notice and a prior hearing, the procedure violated the fundamental principles of due process. The judgment of the Wisconsin Supreme Court was reversed.
sections.Reasoning: Sniadach would eventually get a hearing on the creditor’s claim, but in the meantime she lost the use of wages she had already earned without any chance to present a defense. Summary seizure had been upheld in extraordinary situations, but no such interest appeared here; Sniadach lived in the Wisconsin community, so jurisdiction over her was readily obtainable. Drawing on congressional testimony behind the Consumer Credit Protection Act of 1968, which forbade discharging an employee for a single garnishment, the Court noted that garnishment often cost the debtor a job and always drained family income, that the creditor could add collection fees to the original debt, and that in a vast number of cases the debt was fraudulent, saddled on a poor and ignorant person trapped in an easy-credit nightmare. Prejudgment garnishment of this kind could drive a wage-earning family to the wall, and where the taking is so obvious little argument was needed to show that the procedure violated due process absent notice and a prior hearing.

cp-sniadach.separateOpinions: Justice Harlan concurred: a temporary freeze is a deprivation of the use of the wages, and due process ordinarily requires a hearing on the validity or probable validity of the claim before it. Justice Black dissented, accusing the majority of striking down a state law it thought unwise under a vague natural-law notion of fundamental fairness; Wisconsin’s procedure ultimately gave notice and a hearing, earlier cases such as Ownbey v. Morgan had upheld prejudgment attachment, and the policy choice belonged to the legislature.

cp-fuentes.summary: Statutes letting a private creditor obtain a writ of replevin and have officers seize household goods on a conclusory application and a bond, without a prior hearing, deny due process: a temporary deprivation counts, a buyer’s possessory interest under a conditional sales contract is property, necessities are not the limit, and only truly extraordinary situations justify seizure before a hearing.

sections.Parties: Margarita Fuentes, a Florida consumer whose household goods were seized, was the appellant; Robert Shevin, Florida’s Attorney General, defended the statute, and Firestone Tire and Rubber Company, the seller, was also an appellee. In the companion Pennsylvania case, Parham v. Cortese, consumers whose goods had been seized under Pennsylvania’s replevin statute sued state officials and creditors. The consumers sought declarations that the statutes were unconstitutional and injunctions against their enforcement.
sections.Material Facts: Fuentes bought a gas stove and later a stereophonic phonograph from Firestone under conditional sales contracts, about $500 plus more than $100 in financing; Firestone kept title but she was entitled to possession unless she defaulted. After more than a year of payments, with about $200 left, a dispute arose over servicing the stove and Firestone sued in small-claims court for repossession. Before she received the summons Firestone obtained a writ of replevin, and a deputy sheriff and a Firestone agent seized the stove and stereo from her home. Florida let the writ issue on a conclusory allegation of entitlement and a bond for double the goods’ value; the clerk issued it, and the defendant had three days to post a counterbond. Pennsylvania was more summary still: an affidavit of value and a bond, no suit required, and the person seized against had to sue to get a hearing.
sections.Procedural History: Fuentes sued in federal district court challenging Florida’s prejudgment replevin procedure under the Due Process Clause, and the Pennsylvania appellants brought a similar suit. In each a three-judge district court, then required for suits to enjoin state statutes as unconstitutional, upheld the statute: Fuentes v. Faircloth, 317 F. Supp. 954 (S.D. Fla. 1970), and Epps v. Cortese, 326 F. Supp. 127 (E.D. Pa. 1971). The consumers appealed directly to the Supreme Court, which vacated and remanded on June 12, 1972. Justice Stewart wrote for four Justices (Douglas, Brennan, Marshall); Justice White dissented, joined by Chief Justice Burger and Justice Blackmun; Justices Powell and Rehnquist, who joined the Court after argument, took no part.
sections.Issue: Do statutes that allow a private party to obtain a writ of replevin and have state officers seize goods from another person’s possession, on an ex parte application and a bond, without notice or an opportunity for a hearing before the seizure, violate the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment?
sections.Holding: Yes. The Florida and Pennsylvania statutes were unconstitutional insofar as they denied the right to an opportunity to be heard before chattels are taken from their possessor. To serve its purpose the hearing must come when the deprivation can still be prevented. A temporary, nonfinal deprivation is a deprivation; a buyer’s possessory interest in goods bought under a conditional sales contract is property even though the seller retains title; and due process protects property generally, not only necessities. Seizure without a prior hearing is permitted only in extraordinary situations, absent where only private gain was at stake. The printed clauses permitting the seller to retake the goods did not waive the right to a prior hearing.
sections.Reasoning: When the defendant received the complaint her goods had already been seized on a private party’s say-so, with no state official deciding whether to issue the writ or weighing the need for immediate seizure; the State acted largely in the dark. The right to be heard protects use and possession against arbitrary encroachment and minimizes mistaken deprivations, so it must be honored when the deprivation can still be prevented. Three limiting arguments failed: a counterbond within three days did not make the seizure a non-deprivation, because a temporary deprivation is a deprivation; the buyers’ possessory interest, dearly bought by installments, was property although the sellers held title; and the Fourteenth Amendment speaks of property generally, so courts should not rank which consumer goods deserve protection. Seizure before a hearing is permitted only in truly unusual situations where an important public interest requires very prompt action and a government official decides under a narrowly drawn statute; private gain is not such an interest. Contract language that the seller “may retake” the goods said nothing about waiving a hearing; a waiver of constitutional rights must at least be clear.

cp-fuentes.separateOpinions: Justice White, joined by Chief Justice Burger and Justice Blackmun, dissented: the creditor also has a property interest in installment goods that can be hidden, damaged or depreciate while the defaulting debtor keeps them, defaults are rarely disputed so a prior hearing adds cost and delay for little benefit, and creditors can avoid the decision by adding a hearing waiver to their forms, making the result “no more than ideological tinkering with state law.” Two years later Mitchell v. W.T. Grant upheld Louisiana’s sequestration procedure, and Justice Stewart, dissenting there, said Fuentes had effectively been overruled.

cp-doehr.summary: Prejudgment remedies between private parties are judged by a modified Mathews v. Eldridge test that weighs the defendant’s property interest, the risk of error and value of added safeguards, and principally the plaintiff’s interest; Connecticut’s ex parte attachment of a home on a tort plaintiff’s skeletal affidavit, with no bond, exigency or prior hearing, failed that test as applied.

sections.Parties: John F. DiGiovanni, who was suing Brian K. Doehr for assault and battery, obtained a prejudgment attachment on Doehr’s home; he and the State of Connecticut, which intervened in the Court of Appeals under 28 U.S.C. § 2403(b) to defend its statute, were the petitioners. Doehr, the homeowner, was the respondent, seeking a declaration that the attachment statute violated due process.
sections.Material Facts: On March 15, 1988 DiGiovanni applied to the Connecticut Superior Court for an attachment of $75,000 on Doehr’s home in Meriden in connection with his assault-and-battery suit. The suit did not involve the real estate, and DiGiovanni had no pre-existing interest in the home or any other property of Doehr’s. Connecticut law let a judge authorize prejudgment attachment of real property without a hearing on the plaintiff’s oath that there was probable cause to sustain the validity of the claim, and required no bond. DiGiovanni’s affidavit was five one-sentence paragraphs: the complaint was true, Doehr had willfully and maliciously assaulted him, the assault broke his left wrist and bruised his right eye, he had medical expenses, and in his opinion these facts showed probable cause. A judge found probable cause and ordered the attachment; the sheriff attached the property four days later.
sections.Procedural History: Instead of seeking the post-attachment hearing, Doehr sued DiGiovanni in federal district court under the Due Process Clause. The district court upheld the statute and granted summary judgment to DiGiovanni. A divided Second Circuit reversed in Pinsky v. Duncan, 898 F.2d 852 (1990), Judge Pratt reasoning that the Sniadach line permits postponing a hearing only in exceptional circumstances with added safeguards and that an assault claim turned on disputed facts a judge could not assess on one side’s affidavit; Connecticut intervened after argument under 28 U.S.C. § 2403(b). The Supreme Court affirmed on June 6, 1991. Justice White wrote for the Court in Parts I–III (Rehnquist, Marshall, Blackmun, Stevens, O’Connor, Kennedy, Souter; Scalia joining I and III); Part IV, on bonds, was joined only by Marshall, Stevens and O’Connor; Chief Justice Rehnquist (with Blackmun) and Justice Scalia concurred in part and in the unanimous judgment.
sections.Issue: Does a state statute authorizing prejudgment attachment of real estate without prior notice or hearing, without a showing of extraordinary circumstances, and without requiring the plaintiff to post a bond satisfy the Due Process Clause when invoked by a tort plaintiff who has no pre-existing interest in the property? Must due process also require a bond?
sections.Holding: When a statute lets a private party enlist state power to deprive another of property through prejudgment attachment, the procedure is judged by a modified Mathews v. Eldridge test: the private interest affected; the risk of erroneous deprivation through the procedures used and the value of additional safeguards; and, with principal attention, the interest of the party seeking the remedy, with due regard for any ancillary governmental interest. The Connecticut statute violated due process as applied: the homeowner’s interest was significant, the risk of error substantial, and the plaintiff’s interest in an ex parte attachment minimal because he had no pre-existing interest in the property and alleged no risk that Doehr would transfer or encumber it. A four-Justice plurality would also have required a bond, and held that a bond does not excuse a hearing. The Second Circuit was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: The Court placed the case in the line from Sniadach through Fuentes, Mitchell and North Georgia Finishing and adjusted Mathews’s third factor, the government’s interest, to focus on the interest of the private party seeking the remedy. The private interest was significant: attachment clouds title, impairs sale, taints credit, reduces the chance of a home-equity loan and can put an existing mortgage in technical default, and the Court had never confined due process to complete, physical or permanent deprivations. The risk of error was substantial because attachment rests on a contingency, a future damages award, and Connecticut’s probable-cause standard was obscure, variously described as objective likelihood of success, the plaintiff’s good faith, or surviving a motion to dismiss; under any reading a judge given a skeletal, one-sided affidavit could not realistically assess an assault claim, which unlike a debt does not lend itself to documentary proof. DiGiovanni’s only interest was ensuring assets to satisfy a possible judgment; a supported allegation that Doehr was about to transfer or encumber the property would have been an exigency justifying delay, but he made none.

cp-doehr.separateOpinions: In Part IV, Justices White, Marshall, Stevens and O’Connor would have required a bond, because even a hearing yields only an educated prediction of who will win, while a bond cannot replace a hearing because a lost sale or a lost loan for a child’s education cannot be fully undone by money later. Chief Justice Rehnquist, joined by Justice Blackmun, agreed that the deprivation was significant though the attachment left Doehr in possession, unlike the physical seizures in the earlier cases, and declined to decide hypothetical bond questions. Justice Scalia agreed that an attachment unknown to the common law should be tested under Mathews and failed it.
